IV12-01.solved: NIMBLE = quick and light in movement; 'agile' is the standard one-word equivalent. 'graceful' is beauty of movement, not quickness; 'upright' and 'sturdy' are unrelated senses of bodily bearing.
IV12-01.note: All four adjectives, all common, 2 syllables each except 'graceful'. 'graceful' is the strongest near-miss and is doing real work. Good opener for a form that should start easy.

IV12-02.solved: BOAST = speak with excessive pride about oneself; 'brag' is the exact synonym. complain is negative affect, insist is assertion of a claim, announce is neutral declaration.
IV12-02.note: All verbs. 'brag' is the only informal-register option among three neutral ones, but it is also the only correct one - a very mild register asymmetry, not a tell a student could use without knowing the word.

IV12-03.solved: FORBID = prohibit by authority; 'outlaw' is to make illegal, i.e. forbid by law. review/enforce/delay do not carry prohibition; 'enforce' is nearly the opposite (compelling compliance with, not banning).
IV12-03.note: Register asymmetry worth naming: 'outlaw' is legal-register and is the only option that is also a common noun, while review/enforce/delay are everyday verbs. 'ban' or 'prohibit' would have been a cleaner key. Not disqualifying - the sense match is exact.

IV12-04.solved: SPARSE = thinly dispersed, few and far between. 'crowded together' is the antonym; 'evenly trimmed' and 'newly planted' import a gardening frame the word does not carry.
IV12-04.note: Phrase options, all four adverb+participle, parallel in shape and length. No length or register tell.

IV12-05.solved: BAFFLE = bewilder, confuse; 'puzzle' is the direct synonym. persuade is unrelated; discourage and irritate are affective states, not confusion.
IV12-05.note: All four verbs, all common. Clean.

IV12-06.solved: OBSTINATE = stubbornly refusing to change course; 'unyielding' is the match. unreliable/unconcerned/unhurried are other dispositions entirely.
IV12-06.note: Best-constructed option set in the synonym block: all four share the un- prefix and sit within one syllable of each other, so neither length nor morphology singles the key out.

IV12-07.solved: VIGILANT = keeping careful watch for danger; 'watchful' is the synonym. patient/hopeful/apprehensive are affective, and 'apprehensive' is the fear that vigilance responds to, not vigilance itself.
IV12-07.note: All adjectives, comparable. 'apprehensive' is longer and rarer than the key, which is the safe direction.

IV12-08.solved: LENIENT = not strict in punishing; 'merciful' is the closest of the four. thorough/formal/hesitant describe manner, not indulgence in judgement.
IV12-08.note: 'merciful' is a shade stronger than 'lenient' (mercy implies compassion; leniency implies only mildness) but is unambiguously the only option in the right semantic field. All four adjectives, common.

IV12-09.solved: DIMINISH = become or make smaller; 'dwindle' is to shrink steadily. linger is about duration, stabilize is the absence of change, fluctuate is undirected change.
IV12-09.note: Minor transitivity mismatch: diminish is transitive or intransitive, dwindle is intransitive only, so they are interchangeable only in the intransitive sense. Standard on real ISEE forms. 'fluctuate' and 'stabilize' are genuinely tempting for a student who has 'diminish' as vaguely 'change in amount'.

IV12-10.solved: ARDUOUS = requiring great and sustained effort; 'demanding' is the match. tedious is boring (long, not hard), hazardous is dangerous, unfamiliar is unrelated.
IV12-10.note: 'tedious' is the right kind of distractor - it captures the 'unpleasant, drawn-out' halo of arduous while missing the effort component. All adjectives, comparable register.

IV12-11.solved: SUPERFLUOUS = more than is needed, excess; 'unnecessary' is the direct equivalent. unexplained/uncorroborated/unfinished are about warrant or completion, not surplus.
IV12-11.note: REGISTER FLAG (opposite direction to IV12-14): the key is the only everyday word in the set. 'uncorroborated' is markedly rarer and longer (6 syllables, 14 letters) than 'unnecessary'; a student who knows nothing of 'superfluous' but knows test sets often key a plain word could shortlist B on that alone. Mild, because 'unexplained' and 'unfinished' are also common, so the key is not uniquely short.

IV12-12.solved: PARSIMONIOUS = extremely frugal, stingy; 'unwilling to spend' is exactly that. 'openhanded with friends' is the antonym; 'quick to borrow' and 'unable to save' are different money vices (a spendthrift cannot save - the opposite failing).
IV12-12.note: 'unable to save' is a good trap: a student who reads parsimonious as merely 'bad with money' takes it. Phrase options are parallel; A is the longest at four words against three, a small length asymmetry, but it is a distractor, so it does not help anyone.

IV12-13.solved: INDOLENT = habitually avoiding work; 'lazy' is the plain equivalent. timid/careless/clumsy are other character or competence faults.
IV12-13.note: All four are common adjectives naming a fault, so the key is not singled out by register. 'careless' is the nearest miss (both are failures of application) but does not entail aversion to effort.

IV12-14.solved: CAPRICIOUS = governed by sudden whim, changeable; 'inconstant' is the only option naming changeability. secretive/forgetful/exacting are unrelated traits.
IV12-14.note: REGISTER FLAG - name this one: the key is the only rare/literary word in its set. 'inconstant' (chiefly of affections, and largely archaic outside that use) is less frequent in modern American English than 'capricious' itself, while secretive, forgetful and exacting are all everyday. A student who has learned 'capricious = fickle/impulsive' can still miss this, which makes the item test the DISTRACTOR's vocabulary rather than the stem's. 'fickle' or 'changeable' would be the correct-register key. This is the single worst-matched option set in the synonym block.

IV12-15.solved: The bridge is gone; the printing predates its loss and has not been reissued. A map that reflects a state of affairs that has since changed is out of date.
IV12-15.note: All four options are grammatical predicate adjectives. No polarity tell: crowded is neutral, unofficial/illegible/outdated all negative. 'unofficial' is contradicted by the ranger station being its publisher; 'illegible' by nothing in the stem, which is what makes it weakest.

IV12-16.solved: Read twice before opening, parts laid out in diagram order, finished fast - planning and system, i.e. methodical. 'improvised' is its opposite; 'fortunate' and 'inspired' deny the deliberate preparation the stem itemises.
IV12-16.note: All grammatical. Polarity is mixed on both sides (fortunate and inspired are positive, as is the key), so the key is not identifiable as the odd-valence option.

IV12-17.solved: North wall means no direct sun; the failing bench is the one farthest from the glass; the stem explicitly equalises watering and feeding. Everything but illumination is controlled for.
IV12-17.note: Cleanly constructed: the stem eliminates A and D by name and the geometry selects C over B. Weak point is that 'space' is never addressed at all, so it is eliminated by silence rather than by evidence. Also: a blind solver seeing a greenhouse stem and four resources would guess 'light' on prior alone - the answer is right but not hard to reach without the reasoning.

IV12-18.solved: The card lists ingredients and omits every quantity, temperature and time. A set of directions missing constituent parts is incomplete; the stem's evidence is an enumeration of omissions, which points at the word for missing parts.
IV12-18.second_defensible: C - 'impractical'. A recipe that names ingredients but no amount, heat or duration cannot in fact be cooked from, and 'as a set of directions it is ---' invites a judgement of its usability, not just its contents. A student who reads the final clause as asking 'how does it perform as directions?' reaches impractical by a sound path.
IV12-18.note: The only item in the form where I would not defend uniqueness. 'incomplete' is better - it is the precise name for enumerated omissions, and impractical is the consequence rather than the property - but the gap is a matter of preference, not of one option being indefensible. Fixing it is cheap: drop 'impractical' for something the stem excludes (e.g. 'illegible' or 'unfamiliar'), or change the tag clause to 'the card is ---'. All four options are grammatical and all four are negative, so there is no polarity tell.

IV12-19.solved: 400 at the first meeting, 30 by November - the popularity existed and then did not. 'short-lived' is the only option describing duration.
IV12-19.note: POLARITY FLAG: the key is the only negative option; universal, deserved and deliberate are all neutral-to-commendatory. Combined with 'proved' (which idiomatically precedes a disappointment) the field narrows before the enrolment numbers are read. The numbers make it certain, so the answer is right, but the option set gives it away cheaply. Replacing one distractor with another negative (e.g. 'misleading') would close that.

IV12-20.solved: Amendment requires the vote of EVERY living member; two members on the roll have been unreachable for thirty years, so the required unanimity can never be assembled. The clause meant to protect the document has frozen it.
IV12-20.note: AXIS FLAG - the structurally leakiest item in the form. The stem is entirely about the amendment clause, and only one of the four options mentions amending; 'tiresome to read', 'expensive to enforce' and 'awkward to consult' are about other operations on the document and are not reachable from any wrong path through this stem. A solver who saw the options and only the word 'amended' would pick D. Three same-shape distractors give the surface an appearance of balance that the semantics does not have. Small logical seam worth noting too: if the founders are dead they are not 'living members' and the clause is satisfiable - the stem guards this only by saying they are still carried on the roll.

IV12-21.solved: The label supplies cataloguing data and nothing about content or provenance; measured against a visitor who wants to know what he is looking at, it fails to help. Nothing suggests error, decoration or damage.
IV12-21.note: All grammatical. 'inaccurate' is the useful distractor - it catches students who do not notice that the stem says the label is silent, not wrong. 'ornate' and 'faded' are eliminable without reading the stem carefully, since neither is about information.

IV12-22.solved: Second clause explains each blank in order: three names at the head of the entry = precise about the proposer; 'only that there was discussion' = silent about the opponents. B, C and D all fail the second half; C additionally inverts it ('thorough' contradicts a one-line note).
IV12-22.note: The only two-blank item. All four pairs are grammatical in both slots, and both blanks are load-bearing (no pair can be eliminated on the first word alone except D). 'brief . . . thorough' is a strong trap because it has the right contrastive shape.

IV12-23.solved: It always crossed (one failure in thirty years) = dependable; it never crossed at the same hour twice = not on a regular schedule. The 'but' asks for the quality the tide-dependence costs, which is regularity, not price, speed or comfort.
IV12-23.note: One of the best items here: 'dependable but ---' forces the student to separate reliability from predictability, and all four options are negative so the concessive gives nothing away. Expensive/slow/cramped are eliminable only by noticing the stem never mentions them, which is the correct kind of work.

IV12-24.solved: The rule names lampposts and leaves fences, bus shelters and blank walls untouched, so as an anti-flyposting measure it covers some surfaces and not others - partial. Nothing indicates a sunset clause, illegality, or that it is unenforced gesture.
IV12-24.note: The blank is predicated on 'its coverage', which is what rules out 'symbolic' (a property of the rule, not of coverage) - a student who slides from coverage to rule could reach D, but the stem's grammar blocks it. 'illegal' is grammatical but barely coherent; it is the weak option in the set.

IV12-25.solved: A February count of occupied houses omits summer residents, who are counted elsewhere. So the figure understates August and anyone reading it as a year-round population is misled.
IV12-25.note: 'generous' is a well-built trap that fails on direction: the February count is too LOW for August, not too high. 'unavailable' is eliminated by the fact that a figure was produced. The accurate/--- parallel makes the required polarity clear without making the word obvious.

IV12-26.solved: Erasing and overwriting in the same square destroys the prior value. The ledger therefore preserves the current state of every figure and no history of it - what each figure is, but not what it replaced.
IV12-26.note: The best item in the form - the student must infer that the method's consequence is loss of the superseded value, and no option states that directly. 'means' is a strong distractor for anyone who reads the contrast as data-versus-interpretation; it fails because nothing in the stem concerns interpretation. Small stylistic point: the options mix tense ('means'/'totals' present, 'cost'/'replaced' past), so the two past-tense options pair off and the key is one of a pair of two rather than one of four. All four are grammatical.

IV12-27.solved: Every post-1931 edition copied the one before it, so all of them inherit the 1931 survey's errors; accuracy is capped by what they all derive from. Scale, printing and binding are production properties that cannot add accuracy the underlying survey lacks.
IV12-27.note: All four options are nouns and grammatical after 'than their'. 'scale' is the only distractor with a real claim on accuracy (a coarse scale does limit precision), which makes it the one doing work; printing and binding are eliminable on sight.

IV12-28.solved: By his own stated standard the study needed 400 and had 91, so it does not meet the evidentiary bar he set. 'not so much wrong as ---' asks for a defect of warrant rather than of truth, which is exactly unsupported.
IV12-28.note: I considered 'imprecise' seriously - an undersized sample does widen the interval around an estimate - and rejected it: the stem's object is 'the finding', a qualitative claim, and the named failure is a violation of a sample-size RULE, i.e. a failure of warrant, which 'not so much wrong as' explicitly frames. 'disputed' fails because no dispute appears in the stem, and 'exaggerated' would make it wrong, which the stem denies. All four negative, so no polarity tell. Hardest inference in the form and the one most likely to split strong students; I am confident in A but flagging that C is the distractor to watch if this item's live stats come back at chance.

IV12-29.solved: If the county produced exactly one first novel in four of six years, the winner was the only entrant. Winning then tells you how few competitors there were, not how good the book was - the size of the field.
IV12-29.note: 'the ------- of the field' takes all four nouns grammatically. 'generosity' and 'ambition' are the near-misses for a student who reads the contrast as merit-versus-attitude; the arithmetic of 'exactly one' is what makes size the only supported reading.

IV12-30.solved: A boundary fixed to a movable river becomes indeterminate once the river moves; the clause written to prevent argument is the thing that produced this one. The stem's 'drafted to put the question beyond argument ... has turned out to be' signals an ironic reversal, and only 'origin' completes a reversal.
IV12-30.note: All grammatical after 'the ------- of the dispute'. 'resolution' is the true opposite and is the right trap for a student who misses the reversal; 'exception' and 'record' are not producible from any coherent reading. Good closer - the difficulty is in reading the irony, not in the vocabulary.
